 Indian Economic Policy Is Adrift Without Direction 
 Arun Kumar 
 Cronyism is at the root of the bias in policies that has weakened India’s capacity to deal with the internal and external challenges coming thick and fast. 
 Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. Photo: PTI
 The economy is facing headwinds. The Union external affairs minister recently warned the nation of an impending crisis. The blame for this lies squarely on faulty policy-making that has led to both short-term and long-term challenges. And, when challenges come rapidly, fire-fighting responses do not resolve the underlying cause. That requires a drastic shift in policy.
 Cronyism 
 Elon Musk has accused policy makers of being subservient to oligarchs. Critics have been pointing out that India is practicing crony capitalism, which results in investors not getting a level playing field. As a consequence, not only do they not invest enough in India, but they have also been leaving the country in droves to settle down abroad. 
 Monopolies and oligopolies are present in key sectors like telecom, ports, airports and airlines. The public sector is being asked to vacate the market for the private sector – even in critical sectors like space and defence. ISRO and HAL are being sidelined to favour cronies who are dictating policies. They tried to capture trade in agriculture commodities in 2019 by getting three contentious Bills bulldozed through parliament, which the government was later forced to repeal. 
 Recent major policy announcements point to the helplessness in tackling the challenges. The GST Council has suggested major reforms in the structurally faulty GST – a patchwork at best. The RBI has announced an increase in repo rate by 0.25% and change in Monetary Policy Stance to signal tough steps ahead. Do these steps meet the current challenges facing the economy? 
 Myopic view 
 India is unable to place the economy on a firm footing which would enable it to meet challenges in the short run. The most populous nation is buffeted by external factors – Ukraine war, wars in West Asia, US policies, trade with China, shortages of petro goods and fertilisers. Add to that the threat of Super El Nino and AI.
 The blame lies squarely with the subservience of policy makers to the crony capitalists whose focus is the organised sector and external markets instead of the internal market. This situation has worsened over time because of the vicious cycle it creates between growing inequality and marginalization of the poor who constitute 94% of the workers in the country. If only the market of 6% is catered to, dependence on the external markets rises and India becomes open to external pressures. India has been lured and pushed by International Finance Capital into a vicious cycle of growing inequality and dependence on a narrow market.
 To overcome the US trade challenge, India is entering into FTAs with the UK and EU in a hurry. Negotiations were going on with the EU for 23 years and suddenly an FTA was agreed to. But, India’s experience with FTAs in the last decade has been negative given our technological lag. The FTA partners have been able to increase their exports to us more than we have been able to export to them, thereby enlarging our trade deficit and undermining internal production. This is also likely to happen with the EU because it is a short term fix.
 GST Fix 
 The GST council has announced process reforms, calling it GST 2.0. This has come nine years after the GST was introduced in July 2017. Last September, GST rates were rationalised and reduced.
 Why so late? Since GST was launched, it is common knowledge that it is complex and businesses have found it difficult to cope with it, which has hurt the unorganised sector. There have been innumerable court cases, harassment, fake companies for claiming input credit and corruption. It was stated in the parliament that Rs 70,000 crore of evasion was detected and later a figure of Rs 2 lakh crore was mentioned. What is detected is usually a fraction of the actual occurrence.
 GST was supposed to check the massive tax evasion in indirect taxes. But tax evasion is a joint product of the triad of corrupt businessmen, politicians and the executive (consisting of the bureaucracy and the police). Unless this triad is dismantled the black economy will continue to thrive. Post 1991, so many controls were removed and the tax rates reduced but the black economy continued to thrive. A political consensus is required to keep black economy under check. Without it, process reforms will not achieve much. 
 GST is both structurally faulty and a half-way house compared to the ideal GST. It was brought in under pressure from big business and MNCs. Introduction of VAT in India was a conditionality of World Bank in 1993. It was to help the large and medium scale businesses at the expense of the small and micro sectors. But to make it politically acceptable, features that were pro-poor and pro-backward states were introduced. That made the GST complex. Now it is being simplified without addressing its half-way house characteristic.  
 RBI raising the repo rate will not lower inflation which is due to supply bottlenecks in food and energy, not demand problems. That is in the domain of fiscal policy and not of monetary policy. But, because the government is not willing to collect more direct taxes from the corporate sector and the well-off, it is forced to depend on indirect taxes, which are stagflationary. Since the RBI is mandated to control inflation, all it can do is to squeeze demand which will further slowdown the already stressed economy whose actual growth rate is over stated officially.
 In brief, cronyism is at the root of the bias in policies that has weakened India’s capacity to deal with the internal and external challenges coming thick and fast. The bias results in hurdles that are lowered piece by piece without denting the problem – like flailing in the wind. That is visible when level playing field is not provided to businesses, especially the unorganised sector, in RBI policy for controlling inflation and in a structurally faulty GST damaging the economy. 
 About the Author: 
 Arun Kumar  taught  Economics at JNU and is the author of Indian Economy’s Greatest Crisis: Impact of the Coronavirus and the Road Ahead.
